description:
The fortress of La Zuda was conquered by Ramón Berenguer IV in 1148, later passing to the Knights Templar after being ceded by Alfonso II "the Chaste." King James I of Aragon chose it as his favorite residence, and from here the conquests of Morella, Peñíscola, and Burriana were planned. From 1294, when Tortosa came under direct crown rule, La Zuda became a royal palace, with new halls and defensive elements added.

The Parador de Turismo opened in 1972, giving a new use to much of the old fortress and contributing to its preservation. Today it functions as a magnificent lookout over the Ebro region and Tarragona.

The fortress's Arabic name, "Zuda" or "Suda" (meaning "castle" or "fortress"), preserves a direct linguistic trace of its 10th-century origins predating the Christian reconquest by roughly two centuries.

James I's documented use of La Zuda as a staging point for the conquests of Morella, Peñíscola, and Burriana ties the castle directly to the territorial expansion of the medieval Crown of Aragon.

The castle's position overlooking the Ebro valley gives guests staying at La Zuda sweeping views over one of Catalonia's most significant river landscapes.
